extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors and mathematics educators (teachers of proofs and undergraduate courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Pedagogical guidance and mathematical standards for presenting proofs and topics (e.g., Fourier analysis) to undergraduate/college audiences, emphasizing intuition, examples, alternative proofs, and correct notions of convergence/integrability. Also discusses historical/technical criteria for when Fourier expansions and related manipulations are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use orthogonality to compute Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficient formula for Fourier series follows directly from the orthogonality identity ∫_0^π cos(mx) cos(nx) dx = 0 when m ≠ n (and similar formulae for sines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the orthogonality argument as the simple, direct method for obtaining coefficients rather than convoluted power-series manipulations; emphasize the geometric language (orthogonal/perpendicular) and show the single-line derivation when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require integrability to compute Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourier coefficients of a function f are obtained by integrating f times a sine or cosine; hence f must be integrable for the coefficients to be defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make precise which integral notion is being used (Riemann vs Lebesgue) since more general functions require more powerful integration concepts (Riemann integral may fail where Lebesgue works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet's sufficient condition for pointwise convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function f has a graph with only a finite number of turning points and is smooth except for a finite number of corners and jumps, then its Fourier series converges at each point to the value of f at that point (at jumps, to the average of left and right limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Dirichlet’s criterion to assure students that most 'drawn' curves from physics/engineering satisfy pointwise convergence, but stress that this is a sufficient, not necessary, condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pointwise, almost-everywhere, and L2 convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointwise convergence (valuewise at each x) is distinct from convergence 'almost everywhere' (except on a set of measure zero) and from convergence in L2 (mean-square) sense. For many purposes L2 or almost-everywhere convergence are more natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why pointwise convergence is not the natural mode when changes on measure-zero sets don't affect integrals or coefficients; introduce Lebesgue measure and L2 (Hilbert-space) viewpoints when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square-integrability <=> L2 convergence (Riesz–Fischer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function is in L2 (square-integrable) if and only if its Fourier series converges in the L2 (mean-square) sense; this is the content of the Riesz–Fischer theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Hilbert-space interpretation to make Fourier theory algebraic and transparent: treat functions as vectors with coordinates given by Fourier coefficients and use the Pythagorean analogy for sums of squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointwise divergence can occur even for integrable functions (Kolmogorov caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrability alone does not guarantee pointwise (or almost-everywhere) convergence: Kolmogorov constructed an integrable function whose Fourier series diverges everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn students that integrability is necessary for coefficient definition but insufficient for pointwise convergence; present counterexamples to dispel naive expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carleson's theorem on pointwise convergence for L2 functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function is square-integrable (L2), then its Fourier series converges pointwise almost everywhere (Carleson, 1966).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this landmark theorem to bridge intuition and rigorous result: continuous periodic functions (a special case) have Fourier series converging almost everywhere; yet note remaining pathologies (e.g., divergence sets of measure zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat modifications on sets of measure zero as irrelevant to Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering the values of a function on a set of measure zero does not change its integrals nor its Fourier coefficients; such pointwise changes are 'invisible' to the integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce 'almost everywhere' language early and emphasize that some function spaces (like L2) identify functions that differ only on measure-zero sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalized functions (distributions) to justify formal manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects like Dirac's delta or impulses, and manipulations (e.g., differentiating discontinuous objects), become meaningful in the framework of generalized functions (Schwartz distributions), allowing formal Fourier-style manipulations to be placed on solid footing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching applications (engineering/physics), briefly motivate distributions to explain why physicists' formal calculations (impulses, jumps) can be given mathematical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish convincing examples from rigorous proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of special examples that numerically suggest a pattern (as Fourier's examples did) may be convincing but does not constitute a rigorous proof as understood by mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress to students the difference between experimental/numerical evidence and logical proof; use examples to build intuition but follow with theorems and proofs or counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: When presenting an existential theorem, clarify nonconstructive aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The two-pancake theorem is existential: it guarantees the existence of a bisecting line but does not provide a general constructive method to find it without additional numerical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly tell students whether a theorem is constructive or merely existential and discuss the implications for finding examples or algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build intuition via special cases, lemmas, and visual examples before full generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Before delivering the general proof, present simple, concrete instances (e.g., bisecting circles, overlapping pancakes), prove small lemmas, and show corollaries that set limits and illuminate the general statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use kinesthetic and visual metaphors (pancakes, ham-sandwich) and step-by-step specializations to help students form correct mental models prior to abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid opaque notation and explain measurement/orientation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation such as p(θ), directed distances along rays, or reversed orientations can create confusion if introduced without explanation; students may be insecure with functional notation and directed measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpack notation, define orientation and sign conventions clearly, and motivate why a particular measurement scheme is chosen; consider alternative formulations if a notation creates a 'crisis of understanding.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct discovery or provide alternative proofs to resolve student confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a standard presentation triggers a crisis of understanding, reconstructing the discovery path or producing a different proof that avoids the stumbling step can increase comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document alternative proofs (teacher’s own reconstruction), highlight where the original argument is mysterious, and show a route that confronts the difficulty directly rather than merely repeating the same steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook/monograph presentations should expose honest groping and synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard texts often omit the discovery process and syntheses that aided original understanding; absorbing a page of mathematics is typically a slow, painstaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching, emulate aspects of the discovery process, show failed approaches or motivating questions, and present proofs incrementally to make them accessible rather than assuming instant sight-reading comprehension.
